node.label: Gérard Noiriel
node.date_label: Les Ouvriers dans la société française (1986) · Le Creuset français (1988) · Introduction à la socio-histoire (2006)
node.description: Historian of labour,immigration and state classification whose socio-history follows relationships among identifiable people. In interviews Noiriel presents socio-history as a collective venture rather than a personal school,and treats immigration categories as historically constructed through public language and administrative power. His method connects sociology to archival history while distinguishing explanation from political judgment.

incident_edges.relationship: Noiriel’s socio-history connects archival reconstruction to relationships of power and social interdependence.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2012 opening describes a collective project influenced by sociology,not a claim of sole foundation or institutional membership.

incident_edges.relationship: Noiriel examines how public language and state classification construct immigration as a social and political problem.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2007 interview opening explicitly treats immigration as construction and representation within labour/social history; not denial of actual migration.

incident_edges.relationship: Noiriel explicitly acknowledges Bourdieu’s sociology as an influence on the collective development of socio-history while declining school allegiance.
incident_edges.evidence_note: First 2012 answer. The collective is described by Noiriel as including his own generation and practice; no formal master–disciple relation or adoption of all Bourdieu’s positions is asserted.

incident_edges.relationship: Noiriel criticizes Bourdieu’s later public interventions for presenting political judgments with the undifferentiated authority of researched scholarship.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Second 2012 answer on fundamental research and essays, explicitly naming Raisons d’Agir interventions. This is Noiriel’s critique of the distinction between expertise and public intervention, not a rejection of all Bourdieu’s sociology.

incident_edges.relationship: Noiriel explicitly uses Wittgenstein’s game and language-game metaphor to explain socio-history as shared rules of practice rather than an all-purpose theory.
incident_edges.evidence_note: First 2012 answer, paragraph beginning “La socio-histoire, ce n’est pas une théorie.” A named methodological metaphor, not blanket adoption of Wittgenstein’s philosophy.
